text: Etty left school at 12 and went to work as a printer's apprentice in Hull. Seven years later he moved to London and joined the Royal Academy Schools, where he studied under Thomas Lawrence. His painting Cleopatra's Arrival in Cilicia, shown in 1821, was full of nudes, and it brought him success. He was elected a Royal Academician in 1828, though some people called his nudes indecent. He never married. He retired to York in 1848 and died the following year, shortly after a big exhibition of his work.

Landseer showed his work at the Royal Academy at 13, long before he was old enough to join it. His father was an engraver, and the painter Benjamin Robert Haydon urged him to dissect animals so he could learn how muscles and bones fit together. He became an Academician in 1831 and was knighted in 1850. Queen Victoria gave him many commissions, starting with her pets and moving on to portraits of her babies. He declined the presidency of the Royal Academy. Near the end of his life his family had him declared insane.

Largillière grew up in Antwerp, where his family moved when he was about three. After leaving his first teacher he worked for Peter Lely at Windsor for four years. Charles II wanted to keep him as a court painter, but the Rye House Plot frightened him and he left for Paris. In 1686 he painted a portrait of Charles Le Brun to get into the Académie royale. Le Brun liked it and let him in. James II later offered him the post of keeper of the royal collections, but he said no.

Short started out as a civil engineer and worked on the Thames pollution inquiry before he turned to art. He joined the South Kensington School of Art in 1883. His first successes were etchings and mezzotints after Turner's Liber Studiorum, and John Ruskin gave him praise and advice along the way. Whistler became his friend. Short led the Royal Society of Painter Etchers and Engravers from 1910 to 1938. Low shores and river estuaries held his attention for his whole working life, and he returned to them again and again in his prints.

Liebenwein was keener on animals than on lessons. He left the Vienna Academy in 1891, served in a dragoon regiment, tried a school for historical painting and then followed his friend Ferdinand Andri to Karlsruhe. In Munich he took classes with Heinrich von Zügel, who taught animal painting. From 1897 he worked as an independent painter. On a visit to Burghausen with a friend, he saw the medieval castle, and it impressed them both. He later became vice president of the Vienna Secession and showed with the group many times.

Cranach learned to draw from his father in Kronach, and the family name Maler simply meant painter. In 1504 he joined the court of Frederick the Wise at Wittenberg, and he served the Electors of Saxony for the rest of his life. He became a close friend of Martin Luther, and eleven portraits of the reformer by him survive. His workshop was big, so many pictures exist in several versions. His son Lucas Cranach the Younger kept making versions of them for decades after his death. Nudes from myth and the Bible stayed part of his work throughout his career.

Enea Vico lost his mother at his birth and his father when he was two, and he grew up in a noble family from Parma. He began working young in Parma and Rome, then moved on to Florence and Venice. He engraved grotesques based on antique paintings and made prints for Cosimo I de' Medici. In 1550 he published a book called Donne Auguste while staying at the court in Augsburg. In 1563 he joined the court of Alfonso II d'Este at Ferrara, and he made about five hundred engravings in all. He was also a known numismatist.

Tanner decided to become a painter at about 13, after he watched a landscape artist at work in Fairmount Park. His middle name Ossawa recalled the fighting at Osawatomie between pro and anti slavery groups. In 1879 he enrolled at the Pennsylvania Academy of the Fine Arts in Philadelphia, and he was the only black student there. Thomas Eakins taught him, and Tanner became one of his favorite students. Eakins painted his portrait two decades after Tanner left. In 1891 Tanner moved to Paris to study at the Académie Julian.

Lépine painted the Seine in all its moods for the rest of his life. He grew up in Caen and met Corot in Normandy in 1859, then became his student the following year. He joined the First Impressionist Exhibition at Nadar's in 1874, though people don't usually count him as an Impressionist. His paintings are calm and mostly small. A gold medal at the Exposition Universelle went to his Pont de l'Estacade. He died suddenly in Paris in 1892.

Bernard Picart taught Van der Schley, and he copied his master's style for years afterwards. He mostly engraved portraits and made illustrations, among them pictures for Marivaux's novel La Vie de Marianne, which came out in The Hague over several years. In 1740 he engraved the frontispieces for a 15 volume edition of the works of Brantôme. Most plates in the Hague edition of Prévost's Histoire générale des voyages carry his signature. He worked with Prosper Marchand, who owned many of his prints. He died in Amsterdam in 1779.

Sichem came from a Roman Catholic family of Dutch engravers and publishers that kept the trade going for four generations. He was born in Basel, where his father had moved in 1570 to work as a printmaker. The family went to Amsterdam in 1599. Most of his work was reproductive, which means he cut prints after pictures and prints by others, such as Goltzius, Holbein and Heemskerck. He also made a series of woodcuts of famous people after prints by his father. In 1646 he published a collection of his own work.

Moulijn grew up in Rotterdam as the son of a manufacturer and merchant, and he studied at the academies in Rotterdam and Amsterdam. At the Amsterdam academy he met Richard Roland Holst and Isaac Israëls. After his studies ended in 1887 he wandered between Drenthe, Rotterdam, The Hague and Renkum. The Symbolism of Maurice Maeterlinck strongly shaped his early work. Around 1893 he found his own style. A one man show at S. Bing's gallery in Paris in 1896 was his first big success.

Franco, nicknamed il Semolei, came to Rome from Venice in his twenties. He painted an allegory of the Battle of Montemurlo, which now hangs in the Pitti Palace, and a fresco of the Arrest of John the Baptist in 1541. His style leaned heavily on Michelangelo, but his drawings and etchings have more energy and fresh ideas. Back in Venice he helped paint the ceiling of the Biblioteca Marciana. He also painted panels for the Grimani chapel in San Francesco della Vigna. His son Giacomo became an etcher and publisher.

Carrière decided to become an artist in 1868, when he saw the paintings of Rubens in the Louvre while working as a lithographer. He studied under Alexandre Cabanel, but the Franco Prussian War broke into his studies and he was taken prisoner. His brother found him part time work at the Sèvres porcelain factory, and there he met Auguste Rodin. They stayed close friends. A Salon painting of his earned an honourable mention in 1884, and the critic Roger Marx began to back him. His pictures are done in a nearly one colour brown palette.

Müller saw the Bristol riots of 1831 and recorded some of the scenes in raw, quick sketches. He was born in Bristol, the son of a Prussian museum curator, and studied under James Baker Pyne. In 1838 he set out for Athens, Alexandria and Cairo, then went up the Nile to Luxor to draw the ruins. His scenes of Egyptian streets and markets sold well. Later he travelled to Lycia at his own expense, with his pupil Harry Johnson, and spent three months sketching there. He died in Bristol in 1845, and fakes of his work soon appeared.

Schiavone means the Slav, a nickname for Andrea Meldolla, who was born in Zara in Dalmatia, where his father was a garrison commander, and both of his parents came from Romagna. He taught himself to etch, working at first from drawings by Parmigianino. By 1540 he was established enough in Venice that Vasari commissioned a large battle picture from him. He later influenced Titian, Tintoretto and Jacopo Bassano. Few of his paintings are documented. Vasari says he mostly worked for private clients.

Amsterdam was where Pool lived and died. He worked with Gerard de Lairesse on the engravings for his Groot schilderboeck, and with the painter Barend Graat on prints after ivory sculptures by Francis van Bossuit. In 1708 he married Graat's daughter and moved to the Leidsegracht. Most of his prints copy the work of other artists. He also made topographical views and pictures of the Bentvueghels.

Ismael Mengs, a Danish born painter, raised his son Anton in Dresden and then in Rome from 1741, where he copied Raphael in miniature for the Elector of Saxony. Eight years later the son became first painter to the Elector. In Rome he made a full size copy of Raphael's School of Athens for the Duke of Northumberland. He went to Madrid at the call of Charles III and painted a banqueting hall ceiling in the Royal Palace. Mengs died in Rome in 1779. He left twenty children.

Max kept a herd of monkeys in a garden house in Munich from 1869 to about 1873, and he photographed and sketched them. His mother and sister looked after the animals, but the Munich climate didn't suit them and they died fairly quickly. He later used the material for large paintings in which he sometimes showed the animals as people. He studied with Karl von Piloty at the Munich Academy, and his first critical success came in 1867 with Martyr at the Cross. He also collected between 60,000 and 80,000 objects. Mannheim now has them.

Robert Henri began life as Robert Henry Cozad, and his family changed their names after his father shot a rancher dead in a dispute in 1882. In 1888 he went to Paris and studied at the Académie Julian under Bouguereau. There he came to admire Millet and embraced Impressionism. Back in Philadelphia he drew a group of followers to his studio, among them the illustrators William Glackens, George Luks, Everett Shinn and John Sloan. They called themselves the Charcoal Club. Henri began teaching at the Philadelphia School of Design for Women in 1892.

Wille was the eldest of seven children of a miller, and as a boy he drew birds and the faces of his classmates. When lessons from a local portrait painter went badly, he learned engraving instead and worked for a gunsmith, who taught him to decorate hunting rifles. In 1736 he travelled to Paris as a journeyman. Portraits by Largillière that he engraved caught the eye of Hyacinthe Rigaud, who gave him commissions that made his name. A cannon fired too close to his head cost him his hearing in 1793. He died poor at ninety three.

Cornet ran the print cabinet in Leiden from 1851 until he died in 1882. He had some drawing lessons in his home town but was largely self taught. He often painted scenes from Dutch history, especially the Golden Age, and he added several pictures to Jacob de Vos Jacobszoon's gallery of Dutch history. For his painting of the brothers De Witt, he visited the Gevangenpoort prison in The Hague to copy the room where they were held exactly. He helped found the Lakenhal museum. He was also a director of the Leiden artists' society Ars Aemula Naturae.

Gouda was where Bary lived and died. From his style he seems to have been either a pupil of Cornelis Visscher or someone who formed himself on Visscher's manner. He cut portraits and other subjects very neatly with the graver, though his plates are not equal to Visscher's. His portraits include Erasmus, Hugo Grotius after Mirevelt and an admiral named Ruyter after Ferdinand Bol. He also made prints after Brouwer, Pieter Aertsen and van Dyck. He signed his plates H. Bary and sometimes only H. B.

Shunchō designed Japanese woodblock prints between about 1783 and about 1795. He studied under Katsukawa Shunshō, but his prints of beautiful women look more like the work of Torii Kiyonaga. He was not an innovator. His colours often match Kiyonaga's closely, yet his prints have an ethereal quality and a touch of unsettling mystery in the way they show women. He also designed many shunga prints. Later he studied under Shunman and signed some of his work Kichisadō Shunchō.

Holmes got his start drawing fossil shells and shells of living mollusks for scientists at the Smithsonian Institution. He grew up on a farm near Cadiz in Ohio and went to Washington in 1871 to study art under Theodore Kaufmann. A year later he joined Ferdinand Hayden's government survey as artist and topographer, replacing Thomas Moran. His first trip west took him to the new Yellowstone National Park. In the field he worked closely with the photographer William H. Jackson. In 1879 he went to Munich to study under Frank Duveneck.

Lucas Cranach the Younger trained in his father's workshop in Wittenberg, side by side with his older brother Hans. When Hans died suddenly in 1537, the younger brother took on more responsibility. In 1550 his father left Wittenberg to join the exiled Elector John Frederick I, and from then on Lucas ran the busy family workshop, which kept turning out images of reformers such as Luther. He was never a court painter. Even so, he worked for princes and nobles. He married Barbara Brück in 1541, and they had three sons and a daughter.

Pugin left France around 1798, for reasons that are unclear, and spent most of his adult life in England. He entered the Royal Academy Schools in London and soon found work as a draughtsman for the architect John Nash. Later he made his living as a commercial artist for publishers of illustrated books. With others he drew the plates for Ackermann's Microcosm of London, and he often worked with Thomas Rowlandson. He ran a drawing school at his house in Great Russell Street. In 1823 he and J. Morgan designed the building in Regent's Park that showed Daguerre's dioramas.

Sandrart's uncle Joachim trained him in Amsterdam when he was only ten. After time in Danzig and Regensburg, he married Regina Christina Eimart, the daughter of an engraver, in 1654. The couple settled in Nuremberg two years later and stayed there for the rest of their lives. More than 400 of his engravings survive. He made portraits of leading citizens of Nuremberg, maps, and illustrations for local writers, above all Sigmund von Birken. He also founded the Nuremberg Academy of Fine Arts in 1662 and was its first director.

Mühlig learned painting first from his father Meno, a landscape painter, and his uncle Bernhard was a landscape painter too. He went on to the Dresden Academy of Fine Arts, where he was a master student of Viktor Paul Mohn from 1877. From 1881 he lived in Düsseldorf and painted landscapes and genre scenes. His fields, hunters and walkers on the way to the fair are almost always bathed in bright sunlight. He worked freelance for the art market, not on public contracts. That is why many of his paintings are still in private hands.

Sargent once picked out one of Helleu's paintings and insisted on paying a fair price for it, saying he would never enjoy it as a gift. The two men were close friends for life. Helleu came from Vannes, lost his father in his teens and went to Paris against his mother's wishes. In 1876 he was admitted to the École des Beaux-Arts and trained under Jean-Léon Gérôme. After graduating he hand painted decorative plates for a ceramics firm. There he met Giovanni Boldini, who became a mentor and strongly shaped his style.

Esaias van de Velde's father Hans fled to Amsterdam from Flanders as a Protestant in 1585, and the son was born there. He probably studied under his father and under the landscape painter Gillis van Coninxloo. In 1612 he joined the Haarlem Guild of St. Luke along with Hercules Segers. Adam Elsheimer pushed him toward a more natural look, with a low viewpoint and a triangular composition. He also painted genre and military scenes. He died in The Hague in 1630, where he had been court painter to Prince Maurits and Frederick Henry.

Stachowicz's father was a printer, bookbinder and bookseller in Kraków, and in 1782 the boy joined classes at the Painter's Guild. Five years later he became a master in the guild. In 1816 Bishop Jan Paweł Woronicz gave him a big commission for wall paintings at the Bishop's Palace, which took two years. A fire destroyed them 32 years afterwards. He is best known for pictures of events he saw himself, such as Kościuszko's Oath on the Market Square. He also worked as a lithographer and illustrated a book on the tombs of the Kings of Poland.

Boilly made watercolour caricatures of 73 members of the Institut de France, and his album of them holds the only known portrait of the mathematician Legendre. He was the son of the painter and engraver Louis-Léopold Boilly. He went to the lycée at Versailles, then painted portraits and illustrated books with lithographs. His album of lithographs called Iconographie de l'Institut Royal de France came out in 1820 and 1821. He also collected autographs.

Snyders grew up in Antwerp, where his father kept a wine inn that artists visited. He trained with Hendrick van Balen and became a master of the Antwerp Guild of Saint Luke in 1602. In 1608 he went to Italy, to Rome and then to Milan, where Jan Brueghel introduced him by letter to Cardinal Borromeo. Brueghel asked him to copy a Titian portrait, which shows he was a skilled figure painter before he turned to still lifes. He married the sister of Cornelis and Paul de Vos in 1611. Van Dyck painted him and his wife more than once.

Brascassat took second place in the Prix de Rome of 1825 with a picture of the Hunt of Meleager. He came from Bordeaux. After studying in Paris under Louis Hersent, he went to Italy and painted landscapes that were shown between 1827 and 1835. After that he gave himself mostly to animal painting, and that is what made his name. His Bulls Fighting of 1837 hangs in Nantes, and his Cow Attacked by Wolves is in Leipzig. People knew him for the accuracy of his observation, drawing and painting.

De Morgan studied classical literature and mythology and five languages at home, because her mother wanted her to get the same lessons as her brother. Her paintings centre on the female body and use spiritual, mythological and allegorical themes. She married the ceramicist William De Morgan in 1887, and from 1895 the couple spent half of each year in Florence until the First World War began. She was a pacifist. Her horror at the Boer War and the First World War shows in over fifteen war paintings, including The Red Cross and S.O.S.

Waterhouse picked up the nickname Nino as a boy in South Kensington, where he sketched works in the British Museum and the National Gallery. He had been born in Rome to two painters, and he enrolled at the Royal Academy school in 1871, first to study sculpture. His early pictures had classical themes, in the spirit of Alma-Tadema and Frederic Leighton. In 1874 his painting Sleep and his Half-brother Death hung at the Royal Academy summer show. It was a success. He showed there every year until 1916, except for two years.

De Bisschop was a lawyer before he turned to art, and Houbraken says he worked for the Dutch court. He learned to draw from Bartholomeus Breenbergh, and he later influenced Jacob van der Ulft. Both men came from good families and painted more for pleasure than for a living. He helped found the Confrerie Pictura. For young artists he published two books of instruction, one with 112 prints after ancient statues and another in 1671 with copies after masters. Houbraken says these drawings did the arts a great service.

Schütz started the Collection de 50 vues de la ville de Vienne, a set of fifty engraved views of the churches, palaces and squares of Vienna that Artaria first published in 1779. He took the architectural views of buildings and city districts, while Johann Andreas Ziegler took the suburbs. The plates were coloured by hand in a style that was popular then. Schütz had trained in art and architecture at the Vienna Academy since 1764, and he later taught at the engineering academy. In 1787 he sold Artaria the 17 plates he had engraved so far.

Ancher was the only one of the Skagen Painters who was born and grew up in Skagen, where her father owned the Brøndums Hotel. She studied drawing for three years at Vilhelm Kyhn's school in Copenhagen and later in Paris in the atelier of Puvis de Chavannes. In 1880 she married the painter Michael Ancher. Society said that married women should stay with the household, but she kept painting. She liked interiors and simple scenes from the daily life of Skagen people, especially fishermen, women and children. Light and colour absorbed her, as in Interior with Clematis.

De Wint was the son of an English physician of Dutch descent who had come to England from New York. He was apprenticed to the mezzotinter John Raphael Smith, and in 1806 he bought his freedom by promising to supply 18 oil paintings over two years. That year he visited Lincoln with his friend William Hilton, whose sister Harriet he married in 1810. John Varley gave him lessons. By then he was an established drawing master who spent his summers teaching well off families. Many of his wide landscapes and haymaking scenes are set in Lincolnshire.

Alma-Tadema's father, a village notary in Dronryp, died when the boy was four. The family moved to Leeuwarden, and his mother arranged drawing lessons for her children. It was planned that he would become a lawyer. At fifteen he broke down in body and mind, and doctors diagnosed consumption and gave him little time, so he was allowed to spend his days drawing. He trained at the Royal Academy of Antwerp and settled in London in 1870. In 1873 he was officially recognised as a denizen of Britain.

Henner's painting of Saint Fabiola was copied by artists around the world for devotional use, although the original is now lost. Francis Alÿs has collected over 500 of those copies. Henner won the Prix de Rome in 1858 with a painting of Adam and Eve finding the body of Abel, and in Rome Flandrin guided him. From 1874 he taught at the studio of the ladies, which he ran with Carolus-Duran, because women were not allowed into the École des Beaux-Arts. One of his students was Dorothy Tennant, who later married Henry Morton Stanley.

Zurbarán was nicknamed the Spanish Caravaggio for his forceful use of light and dark. As a child he imitated objects with charcoal, and in 1614 his father sent him to Seville to learn from Pedro Díaz de Villanueva for three years. In 1626 he signed a contract with the Dominican monastery of San Pablo el Real to produce 21 paintings within eight months. Fourteen showed the life of Saint Dominic. That job made his name. In 1629 the elders of Seville invited him to move there for good, and he did.

Harding showed two drawings of buildings at the Royal Academy at 13, in the style of his teacher Samuel Prout. His father was a drawing master and taught him perspective. He left an apprenticeship with the engraver Charles Pye after a year to paint watercolours. He was a popular teacher. In 1841 he published The Park and the Forest, sketched on the stone with a brush in a technique of his own that he called lithotint. He used tinted papers and opaque paints in watercolour, and other painters followed him.

Kunichika's father lost the family bathhouse in Edo, so the family took the mother's surname and the boy became Arakawa Yasohachi. At ten he was apprenticed to a thread and yarn store, but he preferred painting and sketching. At eleven he moved to a shop where he helped design paper lampshades. Around thirteen he became a student of Utagawa Kunisada. His deep knowledge of kabuki led him to make mostly prints of actors and scenes from popular plays. He also drew women and a few landscapes. He worked in the Edo period and carried its ways into the Meiji period.

Brabazon described himself as living for Art and Sunshine. He was born Hercules Brabazon Sharpe, grew up in Paris and graduated in mathematics from Cambridge in 1844. His father wanted him to study law, but he went to Rome to study music and art instead. In 1847 he inherited family estates, and the will required him to take the name Brabazon. He then spent his life travelling and painting, and he saw himself as a gentleman amateur. He did not show or sell his work until his mid seventies, when friends such as John Singer Sargent encouraged him.

La Farge grew up bilingual in New York, and as a child he and his brothers made a handmade magazine in French called Le Chinois. He studied law, but a first visit to Paris in 1856 led him to study painting with Thomas Couture. His first big stained glass job was for Trinity Church in Boston in 1878. In 1880 he got a patent for putting panes of glass on top of each other, and it led to a dispute with his rival Louis Comfort Tiffany.

Brand helped end the baroque era of landscape painting. His father Christian Hilfgott Brand was a German painter who taught in Vienna, and Johann studied at the Vienna Academy from 1736. He received the title Kammermaler and in 1772 became Professor of Landscape Drawing. His landscapes mark the move from the baroque to the 19th century way of showing the countryside. Works by him are held in Laxenburg Castle, the Belvedere in Vienna and the National Gallery in Prague. He died in Vienna in 1795.

Mesdag was a banker's son, and his father, an amateur painter, urged him to study art. He left banking at 35 to paint, after he and his wife Sina inherited a fortune from her father. In 1868 he moved to The Hague to paint the sea. In 1880 a Belgian company asked him for a panorama of Scheveningen, and with the help of Sina and students he made a huge painting, 14 metres high. The company went bust. He bought the painting and paid its losses himself. In 1903 he gave his house and paintings to the Netherlands.

Chartran painted Theodore Roosevelt's official portrait in 1902, and Roosevelt hated it. He hid it in the darkest corner of the White House, his family called it the Mewing Cat, and in the end he had it destroyed and hired John Singer Sargent instead. Chartran came from Besançon, and his parents wanted him to study law or join the army. He chose art and trained under Alexandre Cabanel. A portrait of the Archbishop of Paris on his catafalque won him the Grand Prix de Rome in 1877. For Vanity Fair he drew caricatures signed T.

Abildgaard won the academy's Large Gold Medallion in 1767, which came with a travel grant, but he waited five years to use it. He then spent time in Rome, and with Johan Tobias Sergel and Johann Heinrich Füssli he began to move away from the classicism he had learned. He turned to Shakespeare, Homer and Ossian, and to Greek and Norse mythology. In 1778 he became a professor at the Royal Danish Academy, where he taught mythology and anatomy as well as painting. He also designed Old Norse costumes.

Valadon grew up poor in Montmartre with her mother, an unmarried laundress, and she left school at eleven. She worked in a milliner's shop, a factory making funeral wreaths and a restaurant. At 15 she became an acrobat at the Cirque Fernando, but a fall from a trapeze ended that after a year. She then modelled for ten years or more for Renoir, Puvis de Chavannes and Toulouse-Lautrec, who gave her the nickname Suzanne. She taught herself to draw by watching the artists she posed for. Degas liked her bold line drawings.

Lips was the son of a village surgeon and barber in Kloten. His Latin teacher, the local pastor, introduced him to Johann Caspar Lavater, who persuaded his parents to let him study art. From 1774 he worked with the etcher Schellenberg on the illustrations for Lavater's treatise on physiognomy. He spent much of the 1780s in Rome, where he befriended Tischbein, but he felt trapped there. In 1789 Goethe's recommendation made him a professor at the Weimar drawing school. Five years later a rift with Goethe sent him back to Zürich. He left almost 1,500 engravings.

Alt's father was the painter Jakob Alt, and his older brother was Rudolf von Alt. Franz was born in Vienna in 1821 and died there in 1914. He was an Austrian landscape painter. His works are held by the Metropolitan Museum of Art, the Cooper Hewitt Museum in the Smithsonian, the Albertina in Vienna and the Museum of Fine Arts in Budapest. He painted the Little Castle of the Counts Pejacsevich and the Elisabeth Bridge in Vienna.
